title: Stage 8 Maths — Practice Test 3
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Practice test
summary: A full end-of-Stage-8 practice test in Checkpoint style: Paper 1 (no calculator) and Paper 2 (calculator), 1 hour and 50 marks each, with worked solutions and a mark scheme.

items: This is a full **end-of-Stage-8 practice test** written in the style of Cambridge Lower Secondary tests. It covers the whole Stage 8 curriculum: Number, Algebra, Geometry and Measure, and Statistics and Probability. The Checkpoint test itself is taken at the end of Stage 9; this test prepares you for your Stage 8 end-of-year tests and builds the base for Checkpoint.

**Paper 1:** 1 hour, 50 marks, **no calculator**. **Paper 2:** 1 hour, 50 marks, **calculator allowed**. Answer all the questions. The marks for each part are shown, and most parts are worth 1 or 2 marks.
Equipment: pen, pencil, ruler, protractor, compasses (geometrical instruments), a calculator for Paper 2 only, and tracing paper if you like. Keep squared paper ready for the drawing questions.
The timer starts when you begin a paper. Sit both papers in one session if you can, with a short break between them, exactly as you would on test day.

You may write on paper first if you like, then type your final answer. In the real test you **show all your working** on the paper; marks are given for correct working even when the final answer is wrong.

How marking works here: typed answers (numbers, short answers and multiple-choice) are checked automatically. For written answers, drawings and explanations, you mark yourself at the end using the mark scheme shown with each question. Be strict: give the mark only if your answer matches the mark scheme.
Your score is a **practice score** to help you see your strengths and weaknesses. It is not an official Cambridge result.

blocks.title: Stage 8 Maths — Practice Test 3
blocks.intro: Two papers, 1 hour each, 50 marks each. Paper 1: no calculator. Paper 2: calculator allowed. Diagrams marked NOT TO SCALE must be worked out, not measured. Show your working on paper.

questions.q: (a) Work out  5 + 3 × 2^{2}
questions.e: Indices first: 2^{2} = 4. Then multiply: 3 × 4 = 12. Then add: 5 + 12 = **17**. Common wrong answer: 8 × 4 = 32 (adding first).
(−6) × (−4) = +24 (two negatives make a positive). 24 ÷ (−3) = **−8** (positive ÷ negative is negative).

questions.q:
Find the value of n.
7^{5} × 7^{3} ÷ 7^{8} = 7^{n}
questions.e: Multiply → add the indices: 5 + 3 = 8. Divide → subtract: 8 − 8 = 0. So **n = 0** (and 7^{0} = 1). Do not write n = 1: the value of the expression is 1, but the index is 0.

questions.q: (a) Write 84 as a product of its prime factors.
questions.ms: 1 mark for 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 or 2^{2} × 3 × 7 (factors in any order). Do not accept answers that include 1 or a non-prime factor such as 4 × 3 × 7.
questions.e: 84 = 2 × 42 = 2 × 2 × 21 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7, so **84 = 2^{2} × 3 × 7**. A factor tree or repeated division by primes both work. Check: 4 × 3 × 7 = 84.

questions.q:
(b) At a railway station, a train to Riverside leaves every 12 minutes and a train to Hilltop leaves every 18 minutes.
Two trains, one to each town, leave together at 09:00.
At what time will a train to Riverside and a train to Hilltop next leave together? Show your working.
questions.e:
We need the lowest common multiple of 12 and 18.
Multiples of 12: 12, 24, **36**, 48 …   Multiples of 18: 18, **36**, 54 …
(or 12 = 2^{2} × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3^{2}, so LCM = 2^{2} × 3^{2} = 36.)
09:00 + 36 minutes = **09:36**.
Marking: 1 mark for 36 seen (LCM); 1 mark for 09:36. Common mistake: using the HCF (6) and answering 09:06.

questions.q: Which of these numbers is an integer but **not** a natural number?
questions.e: Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, … Integers are whole numbers, including negative ones. 7 is natural (and an integer); 0.5 and 2/3 are rational but not integers. **−3** is an integer but not a natural number.

questions.q: (a) Work out  ∛(−64)
questions.e: (−4) × (−4) × (−4) = 16 × (−4) = −64, so ∛(−64) = **−4**. Negative numbers DO have a cube root (but not a square root).

questions.q:
(b) Youssef says, '−49 has two square roots: 7 and −7.'
Is he correct? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark for 'No' with a correct reason, e.g. 7^{2} = 49 and (−7)^{2} = 49, so 7 and −7 are the square roots of 49, not −49; OR a square of any number cannot be negative. Do not accept 'No' with no reason.
questions.e: He is **not correct**. 7 × 7 = 49 and (−7) × (−7) = 49. Squaring a positive or a negative number always gives a positive answer, so no number squared gives −49. The two square roots he wrote (7 and −7) belong to **+49**.

questions.q: (a) Work out  46 × 0.01
questions.e: Multiplying by 0.01 is the same as dividing by 100: 46 ÷ 100 = **0.46**.

questions.q: (b) Work out  0.75 ÷ 0.01
questions.e: Dividing by 0.01 is the same as multiplying by 100: 0.75 × 100 = **75**. Check: 75 × 0.01 = 0.75 ✓. Dividing by a number less than 1 makes the answer bigger.

questions.q:
(a) Work out  4 1/3 − 1 3/4
Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form. Show your working.
questions.e:
Estimate: about 4 − 2 = 2.
Method 1 (improper fractions): 4 1/3 = 13/3 = 52/12 and 1 3/4 = 7/4 = 21/12. 52/12 − 21/12 = 31/12 = **2 7/12**.
Method 2: 4 1/3 − 1 = 3 1/3 = 3 4/12; 3 4/12 − 9/12 = 2 16/12 − 9/12 = 2 7/12.
Marking: 1 mark for both fractions over a common denominator (e.g. 52/12 and 21/12, or 4/12 and 9/12); 1 mark for 2 7/12. 31/12 alone scores 1 mark (not a mixed number).

questions.q: (b) Work out  6 × 2 2/3
(c) Work out  5 ÷ 2/3
questions.e: Dividing by 2/3 is the same as multiplying by 3/2: 5 × 3/2 = 15/2 = **7 1/2** (7.5). Check: 7.5 × 2/3 = 5 ✓. The answer is bigger than 5 because we divide by a number less than 1.

questions.q: (d) Which of these fractions is equal to a **recurring** decimal?
questions.e: 3/8 = 0.375, 7/20 = 0.35 and 9/25 = 0.36 all terminate (their denominators have only 2s and 5s as prime factors). **5/6** = 0.8333… = 0.83̇ recurs, because 6 = 2 × 3 has a factor 3.

questions.q:
(a) Write the correct symbol, <, > or =, in the box.
−0.45  ☐  −4/9
questions.e: 4/9 = 0.444…, so −4/9 = −0.444… Now −0.45 is further below zero than −0.444…, so −0.45 is smaller: **−0.45 < −4/9**. Common mistake: thinking 0.45 > 0.444 means −0.45 > −0.444.

questions.q: (b) Work out  0.6 × 0.07
questions.e: 6 × 7 = 42. There are 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places in the question, so the answer has 3: **0.042**. Estimate check: a bit less than 0.1 × 0.6 = 0.06 ✓.

questions.q: (c) Work out  7.2 ÷ 0.3
questions.e: Multiply both numbers by 10 so the divisor is whole: 7.2 ÷ 0.3 = 72 ÷ 3 = **24**.

questions.q:
(a) A youth club raises $1500 at a fundraising evening.
The money is shared between a charity, a club trip and new equipment in the ratio
charity : trip : equipment = 5 : 3 : 2
How much money is given to the club trip? Show your working.
questions.e:
Total parts: 5 + 3 + 2 = 10. One part: $1500 ÷ 10 = $150. Trip: 3 × $150 = **$450**.
(Check: charity $750 + trip $450 + equipment $300 = $1500 ✓.)
Marking: 1 mark for 1500 ÷ 10 or 150 seen; 1 mark for 450.

questions.q:
(b) The club's banner is 40 cm wide and 2 m long.
Write the ratio width : length in its simplest form.
questions.e: Use the same units first: 2 m = 200 cm. 40 : 200, divide both by 40 → **1 : 5**. Common mistake: 40 : 2 = 20 : 1 (units not changed).

questions.q: (a) Simplify  3a^{2} + 5a − a^{2} + 2a
questions.e: Collect like terms: a^{2} terms: 3a^{2} − a^{2} = 2a^{2}; a terms: 5a + 2a = 7a. Answer **2a^{2} + 7a**. a^{2} and a are NOT like terms, so they cannot be added to make 9a^{3} or 9a^{2}.

questions.q: (b) Expand  2x(x^{2} + 5)
questions.e: Multiply each term inside the bracket by 2x: 2x × x^{2} = 2x^{3} and 2x × 5 = 10x. Answer **2x^{3} + 10x**.

questions.q: (c) Factorise completely  12y^{2} + 18y
questions.e:
HCF of 12 and 18 is 6; both terms contain y. So the HCF is 6y. 12y^{2} ÷ 6y = 2y and 18y ÷ 6y = 3. Answer **6y(2y + 3)**. Check by expanding: 12y^{2} + 18y ✓.
Marking: 2 marks for 6y(2y + 3); 1 mark for a correct partial factorisation such as 6(2y^{2} + 3y), 3y(4y + 6) or 2y(6y + 9) ('completely' means take out the HCF).

questions.q: (d) Which one of these is an **equation**?
questions.e: 4n + 7 is an expression (no = sign). P = 2l + 2w is a formula (links several variables; it works for any values). y > 2 is an inequality. **3t − 5 = 16** is an equation: it is true for one value of t only (t = 7).

questions.q:
(a)  5x − 7 = 2x + 8
Show your working.
questions.e:
Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x − 7 = 8. Add 7: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: **x = 5**. Check: 5 × 5 − 7 = 18 and 2 × 5 + 8 = 18 ✓.
Marking: 1 mark for a correct first step that collects x terms or numbers (e.g. 3x − 7 = 8 or 3x = 15); 1 mark for x = 5.
Subtract 3: x/4 = −2. Multiply by 4: **x = −8**. Check: −8 ÷ 4 + 3 = −2 + 3 = 1 ✓.

questions.q: Write down the inequality shown, using x.
questions.e: An open (empty) circle means the number is NOT included: x > −2, written −2 < x. A filled circle means it IS included: x ≤ 3. Together: **−2 < x ≤ 3**.

questions.q:
(a) The first term of a sequence is 3/4. The term-to-term rule is 'add 1/2'.
Work out the 4th term. Give your answer as a mixed number.

(b) Here are the first four terms of another sequence.
7,   4,   1,   −2,   …
Find an expression for the nth term.
questions.e:
The terms go down by 3 each time, so the nth term starts with −3n. When n = 1, −3n = −3, and we need 7, so add 10. nth term = **10 − 3n** (or −3n + 10). Check n = 4: 10 − 12 = −2 ✓.
Marking: 2 marks for 10 − 3n oe; 1 mark for −3n + c with c ≠ 10, or for 10 − 3n written as a term-to-term rule. Common mistake: n − 3 (that is the term-to-term rule idea, not the nth term).

questions.p:
Question 14
Here is a function machine.
input → [ × 3 ] → [ − 5 ] → output
questions.q:
(b) Find the input when the output is −3.
Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.e: Work backwards with inverse operations: −3 + 5 = 2, then 2 ÷ 3 = **2/3**. Check: 2/3 × 3 = 2, 2 − 5 = −3 ✓.

questions.q: (a) Which line has gradient −2 and crosses the y-axis at (0, 5)?
questions.e: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept. m = −2 and c = 5 give **y = −2x + 5**.

Then draw the graph of y = 2x − 3 for values of x from −1 to 3 on a copy of this grid.

questions.ms: 1 mark for a complete reason using correct vocabulary, e.g. 'corresponding angles are equal AND angles on a straight line add up to 180°', OR 'vertically opposite angles are equal AND co-interior angles add up to 180°', OR 'alternate angles are equal and angles on a straight line add up to 180°'. Do not accept 'F angles', 'Z angles' or 'parallel lines' on its own.
questions.e: Corresponding angles are equal, so the angle at the lower crossing in the same position as 64° is 64°. Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so y = 180° − 64° = 116°. Always use the proper words: corresponding, alternate, vertically opposite, angles on a straight line.

questions.q:
(a) A mosque courtyard has a fountain in its centre. From above, the fountain is a regular octagon.
Write down the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of a regular octagon.
questions.ms: 1 mark for BOTH: 8 lines of symmetry AND rotational symmetry of order 8.
questions.e: A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n. An octagon has 8 sides, so it has **8 lines of symmetry** (4 through opposite corners and 4 through the midpoints of opposite sides) and **rotational symmetry of order 8** (it looks the same after every turn of 360° ÷ 8 = 45°).

questions.q:
(b) The courtyard floor is decorated with quadrilaterals.
Which statement is **always** true?
questions.e: A square has four right angles and two pairs of parallel sides, so it has every property of a rectangle: **a square is always a rectangle**. A rhombus need not have right angles; a trapezium may have only one pair of parallel sides; a kite need not have four equal sides.

questions.q:
(c) A lantern in the courtyard is a polyhedron with 12 vertices and 18 edges.
Use Euler's formula to work out the number of faces of the lantern.
questions.e: Euler's formula: F + V − E = 2. So F + 12 − 18 = 2 → F − 6 = 2 → **F = 8**. (This is a hexagonal prism: 2 hexagons + 6 rectangles.)

questions.q: Describe fully the **single** transformation that maps triangle A onto triangle B.
questions.ms: 1 mark for 'reflection'; 1 mark for 'in the line y = x'. Also accept, for full marks, 'rotation of 180° about (3, 3)' — because this triangle is isosceles, this rotation also maps A exactly onto B. Do not accept 'flip' or 'mirror'. A combination of two transformations scores 0.
questions.e: **Reflection in the line y = x.** Check each vertex: (1, 3) → (3, 1), (1, 5) → (5, 1), (3, 5) → (5, 3). Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates: (a, b) → (b, a). Each point and its image are the same distance from the line y = x.

questions.p:
Question 20
In a board game, a player spins a fair spinner numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and rolls a fair six-sided dice numbered 1 to 6.
questions.q:
(a) In this game, the probability that a player lands on a 'bonus' square on a turn is 0.18.
Work out the probability that the player does **not** land on a bonus square.
questions.e: Landing on a bonus square and not landing on one are complementary events, so their probabilities add up to 1: 1 − 0.18 = **0.82**.

questions.p:
Question 20
In a board game, a player spins a fair spinner numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and rolls a fair six-sided dice numbered 1 to 6.
questions.q:
(b) The player adds the number on the spinner and the number on the dice.
Work out the probability that the total is 7. Show your working.
questions.e:
There are 4 × 6 = 24 equally likely outcomes (use a sample-space table: spinner 1–4 down the side, dice 1–6 across the top).
Totals of 7: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3) → 4 outcomes.
P(total 7) = 4/24 = **1/6**.
Marking: 1 mark for 24 outcomes or the 4 correct pairs seen; 1 mark for 4/24 oe. Common mistake: counting only the possible totals 2 to 10 (9 totals) as if they were equally likely.

questions.p:
Question 1
An online shop is having a sale.
questions.q:
(a) A jacket normally costs $64. In the sale its price is reduced by 15%.
Work out the sale price of the jacket, in dollars. Show your working.
questions.e:
Multiplier method: 100% − 15% = 85% = 0.85. 64 × 0.85 = **$54.40**.
Or: 15% of 64 = 9.60, then 64 − 9.60 = 54.40.
Marking: 1 mark for 64 × 0.85 or 9.6 seen; 1 mark for 54.40 (accept 54.4). Common mistake: 64 − 15 = 49.

questions.p:
Question 1
An online shop is having a sale.
questions.q:
(b) After the sale, the price of a pair of headphones goes up from $48 to $54.
Work out the percentage increase. Show your working.
questions.e:
Absolute change = 54 − 48 = $6. Percentage increase = change ÷ ORIGINAL × 100 = 6 ÷ 48 × 100 = **12.5%**.
Marking: 1 mark for 6/48 seen (or 54/48 = 1.125); 1 mark for 12.5. Common mistake: dividing by the new price, 6 ÷ 54 × 100 = 11.1%.

questions.p:
Question 1
An online shop is having a sale.
questions.q:
(c) The price of a pencil case rises from $20 to $25.
The price of a school bag rises from $80 to $92.
Hana says, 'The price of the school bag increased more.'
Explain why Hana is correct in one way but not correct in another way. Show your working.
questions.ms: 1 mark for the absolute changes: bag $12 and pencil case $5, so the bag increased more in dollars. 1 mark for the percentage changes: pencil case 25% and bag 15%, so the pencil case increased more in percentage terms. Accept 25/20 = 1.25 and 92/80 = 1.15 for the second mark.
questions.e:
Absolute change: bag 92 − 80 = $12; pencil case 25 − 20 = $5. In dollars, Hana is correct: the bag went up more.
Percentage change: pencil case 5 ÷ 20 × 100 = 25%; bag 12 ÷ 80 × 100 = 15%. Compared with its original price, the pencil case went up more, so Hana is not correct in percentage terms.

questions.q:
(a) The online shop sells rice in two pack sizes.
Pack A: 750 g for $4.20
Pack B: 1.2 kg for $6.60
Which pack is better value for money? Show your working.
questions.ms: 1 mark for two values that can be compared, using the same units, e.g. $5.60 per kg and $5.50 per kg; OR 56 cents and 55 cents per 100 g; OR 178.6 g and 181.8 g per dollar. 1 mark for 'Pack B' with correct supporting values. 'Pack B' with no working scores 0.
questions.e:
Change to the same units: 750 g = 0.75 kg.
Pack A: 4.20 ÷ 0.75 = $5.60 per kg.  Pack B: 6.60 ÷ 1.2 = $5.50 per kg.
Pack B costs less per kilogram, so **Pack B** is better value.
Common mistake: comparing 4.20 ÷ 750 with 6.60 ÷ 1.2 (different units).

questions.q:
(b) 5 m of garden hose costs $13.75. The cost is directly proportional to the length.
Work out the cost of 8 m of the same hose.

questions.p:
Question 3
A passenger train runs between several towns.
questions.q:
(a) In one week the train travelled 6847.5 km.
Round 6847.5 to 2 significant figures.
questions.e: The first two significant figures are 6 and 8 (6800…). The next digit is 4, which is less than 5, so round down: **6800** km. Keep the zeros to hold the place value: 68 is wrong.

questions.p:
Question 3
A passenger train runs between several towns.
questions.q:
(b) The distance between two of the towns is 45 miles.
Use 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km to change 45 miles into kilometres.
questions.e: 45 × 1.6 = **72 km**. A kilometre is shorter than a mile, so the number of kilometres must be bigger.

questions.p:
Question 3
A passenger train runs between several towns.
questions.q:
(c) The whole route is 120 km long.
Use 1 km ≈ 5/8 mile to change 120 km into miles.
questions.e: 120 × 5/8 = 600 ÷ 8 = **75 miles**. (Check with the other fact: 75 × 1.6 = 120 ✓.)

(a) A water trough on a farm is a triangular prism.
Work out the volume of the trough. Show your working.
questions.e:
Area of the triangular cross-section = ½ × base × height = ½ × 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.48 m^{2}.
Volume = area of cross-section × length = 0.48 × 2.5 = **1.2 m^{3}**.
Marking: 1 mark for 0.48 seen (or ½ × 1.2 × 0.8 × 2.5 seen); 1 mark for 1.2. Common mistake: 1.2 × 0.8 × 2.5 = 2.4 (forgetting the ½).

questions.q:
(b) A water trough on a farm is a triangular prism.
1 m^{3} = 1000 litres.
How many litres of water does the full trough hold?
questions.e: 1.2 × 1000 = **1200 litres**. (Follow through: 1000 × your answer to part (a).)

questions.q:
(c) A closed water tank is a cuboid 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 1.2 m high.
The outside of the tank is painted. Work out its total surface area. Show your working.
questions.e:
There are three pairs of equal faces:
2 × 1.5 = 3 m^{2};  2 × 1.2 = 2.4 m^{2};  1.5 × 1.2 = 1.8 m^{2}.
Total = 2 × (3 + 2.4 + 1.8) = 2 × 7.2 = **14.4 m^{2}**.
Marking: 1 mark for at least two of 3, 2.4, 1.8 seen; 1 mark for 14.4. Common mistake: 7.2 (only one face of each pair).

questions.q:
(c) For 15 girls at the same car wash, the median amount was $33 and the range was $18.
Make two comparisons between the amounts collected by the boys and the girls.
questions.ms: 1 mark for comparing averages in context: the girls' median ($33) is higher than the boys' ($29), so on average the girls collected more. 1 mark for comparing spread in context: the girls' range ($18) is smaller than the boys' ($36), so the girls' amounts were more consistent / less spread out. FT their (a) and (b). Do not accept statements that only quote the numbers without saying what they mean.
questions.e:
Average: the girls' median, $33, is greater than the boys' median, $29, so **on average the girls collected more money**.
Spread: the girls' range, $18, is smaller than the boys' range, $36, so **the girls' amounts were more consistent** (less spread out).

questions.q:
(a) Altogether, the youth club raised $2400 this year. It gave $1080 of this to charity.

(b) The club has 240 members. The leader wants to know which activities the members would like next term. He decides to ask a sample of members.
Which sample is **least** likely to be biased?
c: Choose 30 members at random from the full list of 240 members
Ask the first 20 members who arrive on Friday evening
Ask 20 members of the club's football team
Ask the leader's own friends in the club
questions.e: A **random sample from the full list** gives every member the same chance of being chosen. The other samples only include certain kinds of member (early arrivals, footballers, the leader's friends), whose views may not represent the whole club.

questions.q:
(c) The club has 240 members. The leader wants to know which activities the members would like next term. He decides to ask a sample of members.
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of asking a sample instead of asking all 240 members.
questions.ms: 1 mark for BOTH: an advantage (e.g. quicker / cheaper / easier to collect and analyse) AND a disadvantage (e.g. may not represent all members / results less reliable / some opinions are missed).
questions.e:
Advantage: a sample is **quicker and easier** to collect and analyse than asking everyone.
Disadvantage: the sample **might not represent all 240 members**, so the results may be less reliable than asking everybody.

questions.q:
(a) At the youth club quiz night, an adult ticket costs $x and a child ticket costs $4 less than an adult ticket.
A family buys 2 adult tickets and 3 child tickets. They pay $43 altogether.
Show that 5x − 12 = 43.
questions.ms: 1 mark for a correct expression for the total cost, e.g. 2x + 3(x − 4) = 43, expanded to reach 5x − 12 = 43 with no errors.
questions.e: A child ticket costs x − 4 dollars. Total: 2x + 3(x − 4) = 43 → 2x + 3x − 12 = 43 → **5x − 12 = 43**.

questions.q:
(b) At the youth club quiz night, an adult ticket costs $x and a child ticket costs $4 less than an adult ticket.
A family buys 2 adult tickets and 3 child tickets. They pay $43 altogether.
Solve the equation to find the cost of an adult ticket.
questions.e: 5x − 12 = 43 → 5x = 55 → **x = 11**. An adult ticket costs $11 (and a child ticket $7). Check: 2 × 11 + 3 × 7 = 22 + 21 = 43 ✓.

questions.q:
(c) The online shop uses this formula for the delivery cost, C dollars, of a parcel with a mass of w kilograms:
C = 4.5 + 0.8w
Work out the delivery cost for a parcel with a mass of 12.5 kg.

(d) The online shop uses this formula for the delivery cost, C dollars, of a parcel with a mass of w kilograms:
C = 4.5 + 0.8w
Rearrange the formula to make w the subject.
questions.ms: 1 mark for w = (C − 4.5) ÷ 0.8 oe, e.g. w = (C − 4.5)/0.8, w = 1.25(C − 4.5), w = 1.25C − 5.625. Brackets must be correct: do not accept w = C − 4.5 ÷ 0.8.
questions.e: Subtract 4.5 from both sides: C − 4.5 = 0.8w. Divide both sides by 0.8: **w = (C − 4.5) ÷ 0.8** (which is the same as 1.25(C − 4.5)). Check with part (c): (14.5 − 4.5) ÷ 0.8 = 12.5 ✓.

questions.q:
(e) The youth club has p members. Two-thirds of the members go on a trip, and 5 leaders go with them.
Write an expression, in terms of p, for the total number of people who go on the trip.
questions.e: Two-thirds of p is (2/3)p, also written 2p/3. Add the 5 leaders: **(2/3)p + 5**. Common mistake: 2/3 + p + 5 or 2/3(p + 5).

questions.q:
(a) Triangle T has vertices at (2, 3), (3, 3) and (2, 5).
T is enlarged by scale factor 3, with centre of enlargement (1, 1).
Write down the coordinates of the image of the vertex (2, 5).
questions.e: From the centre (1, 1) to (2, 5) is 1 right and 4 up. Multiply by the scale factor 3: 3 right and 12 up. From (1, 1): (1 + 3, 1 + 12) = **(4, 13)**. Common mistake: multiplying the coordinates by 3 from the origin, giving (6, 15).

questions.ms: 1 mark for 'rotation' with '90° clockwise' (accept 270° anticlockwise); 1 mark for 'centre (0, 0)' or 'about the origin'. Only 1 mark in total if two different transformations are given.
questions.e: **Rotation, 90° clockwise, centre (0, 0).** Check: (1, 1) → (1, −1), (4, 1) → (1, −4), (1, 3) → (3, −1). A rotation needs three facts: the centre, the angle and the direction. Use tracing paper to check: trace R, put your pencil on (0, 0) and turn a quarter-turn clockwise.

questions.q:
(a) On a plan of the mosque courtyard, the bearing of the minaret from the gate is 125°.
Work out the bearing of the gate from the minaret.
questions.e: The back bearing differs by 180°: 125° + 180° = **305°**. (If the bearing is more than 180°, subtract 180° instead.) Draw a sketch with north lines at both points to check.

questions.q:
(b) On the same plan, a straight path goes from (−3, 5) to (7, −1). A lamp is placed at the midpoint of the path.
Find the coordinates of the lamp.
questions.e: Midpoint = (mean of the x-coordinates, mean of the y-coordinates) = ((−3 + 7) ÷ 2, (5 + (−1)) ÷ 2) = (4 ÷ 2, 4 ÷ 2) = **(2, 2)**.

questions.p:
Question 13
A triangular flower bed in the courtyard is drawn to scale as triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm.
questions.q: On paper, use a ruler and compasses only to construct triangle ABC. Leave in your construction arcs.
questions.ms: 1 mark for AB drawn 7 cm (±1 mm) with an arc of radius 5 cm from A or 6 cm from B. 1 mark for a complete correct triangle with both arcs shown and sides within ±1 mm. Do not award the second mark if no arcs are visible.
questions.e:
1. Draw AB = 7 cm with a ruler.
2. Open the compasses to 5 cm; with the point on A, draw an arc above AB.
3. Open the compasses to 6 cm; with the point on B, draw an arc that crosses the first arc. The crossing point is C.
4. Join AC and BC with a ruler. Do not rub out the arcs: they show your method.
Check: measure AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm (angle A should be about 57°).

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the worked solution for every question, including the ones you got right, and check that your method matches. In the real test the working earns marks too.
Mark your written answers honestly with the mark scheme. If you are not sure whether an answer earns the mark, do not give it.
Make a list of the questions you lost marks on, and next to each one write the topic tag and what went wrong (a rule you forgot, a careless slip, misreading the question, running out of time).

Number mistakes: revisit 'Order of Operations and Calculating with Integers', 'Factors, Multiples, Primes, HCF and LCM', 'Fractions: Recurring Decimals, Mixed Numbers and Order of Operations', 'Percentage Increase, Decrease and Absolute Change' and 'Ratio and Proportion'.

Algebra mistakes: revisit 'Algebraic Expressions: Simplifying, Expanding and Factorising', 'Equations and Inequalities', 'Writing Expressions and Formulae, and Changing the Subject', 'Sequences and the nth Term' and 'Reading and Interpreting Real-life Graphs'.

Geometry mistakes: revisit 'Angles in Triangles and on Parallel Lines', 'Area of Parallelograms and Trapezia', 'Volume of Prisms and Surface Area', 'Circumference of a Circle, and Miles and Kilometres', '3D Shapes: Euler's Formula and Plans and Elevations' and 'Translation, Reflection, Rotation and Enlargement'.
Statistics and probability mistakes: revisit 'Averages, Range and Comparing Distributions', 'Data Collection and Sampling' and 'Probability: Complementary and Combined Events'.
After two weeks of revision, try Practice Test 1 or 2 and compare your scores paper by paper.
